SEMINAR WORKSHEET SESSION 02 SUSTAINABLE CITIES B1/B2 COMMUNICATIVE LAB

Sustainable Cities & Low-Emission Mobility

Urban Living, Green Neighborhoods, The 15-Minute City & Car-Free Center Debate

Session Learning Objectives

• Urban Microclimates: Explain the Urban Heat Island effect, sponge city principles, and 15-minute urban planning using clear B2 sentence stems.
• Photo Contrast: Compare 4 contrasting images of urban transit: car sprawl, pedestrian superblocks, rail corridors, and micro-mobility streets.
• Double Comparatives: Master proportional change structures (The denser... the lower...) and formal contrast connectors (whereas, nevertheless, despite).
• Collocation Game: Match 10 compound mobility collocations and analyze the Sustainable Mobility Hierarchy pyramid.
• Redesign Sprint: Re-engineer an 8-lane airport corridor into a multimodal green district and deliver a 90-second pitch.
• Public Debate: Debate a permanent ban on private fossil-fueled vehicles from the central district across 3 stakeholder roles.

Part 1: Livable City Ranking & Diagnostic Warm-up (Pairwork)

Rank the following 5 factors of a truly livable city from 1 (most essential) to 5 (least essential). Compare with your partner:

A. Bike Lanes
Safe, segregated cycle network across metropolitan area.
B. Green Parks
Public canopy & gardens within 5 min of every front door.
C. Rapid Transit
Affordable electric trams & metros running frequently.
D. Car-Free Zones
Pedestrianized shopping streets with zero traffic noise.
E. Sponge Drainage
Permeable streets preventing catastrophic urban runoff.

Essential Spoken Vocabulary: 18 Sustainable Mobility Terms

CORE B1/B2 GLOSSARY
1. 15-Minute City /ˈfɪftiːn ˈmɪnɪt ˈsɪti/
Urban planning concept where work, food, and health are reachable within 15 minutes on foot or bike.
2. Active Mobility /ˈæktɪv məʊˈbɪləti/
Human-powered physical travel, primarily walking, wheeling, and cycling.
3. Low-Emission Zone /ləʊ ɪˈmɪʃn zəʊn/
Designated urban area where high-polluting vehicles are fined or banned completely.
4. Sponge City /spʌndʒ ˈsɪti/
City built with wetlands, rain gardens, and permeable soil that absorbs and reuses rainwater.
5. Permeable Pavement /ˈpɜːmiəbl/
Porous surface materials allowing stormwater to infiltrate naturally into underlying aquifers.
6. Multimodal Transit /ˌmʌltiˈməʊdl/
Seamless travel combining trains, buses, e-bikes, and walking under a single integrated fare card.
7. Heat Island Effect /hiːt ˈaɪlənd/
Phenomenon where concrete and tarmac absorb solar radiation, making cities 4–8°C hotter than rural areas.
8. Traffic Calming /ˈtræfɪk ˈkɑːmɪŋ/
Physical design interventions like speed humps, chicanes, and narrowings that force drivers to slow down.
9. Superblock /ˈsuːpəblɒk/
Neighborhood unit (pioneered in Barcelona) where cars are restricted to perimeter roads.
10. Micro-Mobility /ˈmaɪkrəʊ məʊˈbɪləti/
Small, lightweight personal transport like shared e-bikes, cargo bikes, and electric kick-scooters.
11. Light Rail Transit /laɪt reɪl/
Modern electric tramways operating in segregated median lanes with high passenger capacity.
12. Park-and-Ride /pɑːk ænd raɪd/
Perimeter parking garage where suburban drivers leave their cars and transfer to rapid rail or bus transit.
13. Pedestrianization /pəˌdestriənaɪˈzeɪʃn/
Converting vehicular streets into car-free public zones dedicated to pedestrians, cafes, and trees.
14. Congestion Charge /kənˈdʒestʃən tʃɑːdʒ/
Daily financial levy charged to motorists entering a crowded city center during peak hours.
15. Bus Rapid Transit /bʌs ˈræpɪd/
High-frequency bus system running on dedicated rights-of-way with off-board ticketing.
16. Carbon Neutral /ˈkɑːbən ˈnjuːtrəl/
Balancing emitted greenhouse gases with equivalent carbon absorption or renewable offsets.
17. Bicycle Corridor /ˈbaɪsɪkl ˈkɒrɪdɔː/
Continuous, protected cycle highway connecting outer residential districts directly to city employment.
18. Livability Index /ˌlɪvəˈbɪləti/
Comparative ranking of cities assessing air quality, public safety, transit, and green public space.

Part 2: 4-Photo Visual Contrast & Debate Lab — Two Visions of the Future City

Work in pairs. Contrast two competing urban philosophies: car-centric congestion vs. human-scale livability and clean transit.

Photo A: The Car-Choked Highway URBAN SPRAWL

8-lane arterial motorway dividing neighborhoods; exhaust pollution, noise, and stationary gridlock.

Debate Question: Does building wider motorways reduce traffic congestion, or does it simply induce more demand?
Photo B: The Reclaimed Superblock BARCELONA MODEL

Former asphalt intersection converted into tree canopies, children's play areas, and outdoor cafes.

Debate Question: How can cities protect local shopkeepers when street parking is converted into pedestrian plazas?
Photo C: High-Speed Rail Corridor INTERMODAL TRANSIT

High-speed electric train connecting city centers in 2 hours, replacing carbon-heavy domestic flights.

Debate Question: Should governments legally ban short-haul domestic flights where high-speed rail takes under 2.5 hours?
Photo D: The 15-Minute Micro-Mobility Street HUMAN-SCALE LIVING

Mixed-use street with protected cycle lanes, electric cargo bikes, grocery shops, and shaded benches.

Debate Question: Is the 15-minute city realistic for outer suburbs, or only wealthy metropolitan centers?

Sentence Stems for Contrasting Urban Environments

"Photo A represents 20th-century car dependency, whereas Photo B shows street space reclaimed for humans."
"The more road capacity we build for private vehicles, the more traffic gridlock we inevitably generate."
"Photo C illustrates rail as an intermodal alternative to aviation, cutting emissions by up to 90%."
"Photo D embodies the 15-minute city philosophy: daily necessities accessible without touching a car steering wheel."

Paired Discussion & Urban Design Verdict

Discuss with your partner: If you were mayor of your hometown, which of these 4 environments would you prioritize funding first, and why?

Part 3: Spoken Language Clinic — Proposing Solutions & Double Comparatives

Mastering proportional changes (The more... the less...) and formal contrast connectors in urban policy proposals.

1. Double Comparative Formulas (Proportionality)

Show that one change directly causes another to increase or decrease:

"The denser the transit network, the fewer private cars enter the city center."
"The more protected cycle tracks we build, the safer commuters feel."
"The cheaper the train tickets, the more likely passengers choose rail over air."
"The higher the parking fees, the less congestion we observe."

2. Formal Contrast Connectors

Balance opposing arguments diplomatically:

"Whereas cars consume 70% of street space, they move under 30% of commuters."
"Despite initial merchant resistance, pedestrian zones boosted retail profits by 15%."
"Electric trams have high upfront costs; nevertheless, their life-cycle emissions are zero."
"While suburbs need road access, inner districts must prioritize human health."

Communicative Transformation Practice

Work in pairs. Combine the two statements into a single, polished B2 sentence using double comparatives or contrast linkers:

1. Cities plant more shade trees. The urban heat island effect drops dramatically.
→ The more shade trees cities plant, the lower the urban heat island effect drops.
2. Public transit is made frequent and affordable. Commuters abandon their cars.
3. Electric cargo bikes are clean and agile. Delivery companies still rely on diesel vans.
4. Airports invest heavily in intermodal rail links. Airport car park revenue declines.

The Sustainable Mobility Hierarchy (Modal Pyramid)

Analyze the inverted hierarchy below. How does your daily commute compare to this recommended sustainability ladder?

1. ACTIVE MOBILITY (Walking, Wheeling, Cycling) • ZERO EMISSIONS • HIGHEST SOCIAL EFFICIENCY
2. MASS ELECTRIC TRANSIT (High-Speed Trains, Metros, Modern Tramways) • HIGH CAPACITY
3. SHARED MICRO-MOBILITY & ELECTRIC BUSES • FLEXIBLE FIRST/LAST-MILE SOLUTIONS
4. CARPOOLING & SHARED ELECTRIC VEHICLES • REDUCED URBAN FOOTPRINT
5. SINGLE-OCCUPANCY PRIVATE FOSSIL CARS • HIGHEST POLLUTION & SPACE WASTE

Part 5: Pair Urban Redesign Challenge — The 15-Minute Airport District

Scenario: You are transport planners commissioned to transform an 8-lane highway corridor connecting the regional airport to the neighboring suburbs.

Intervention 1: Lane Reallocation

Convert 4 of the 8 car lanes into:

Dedicated bi-directional Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) lane + wide protected cycle track.

Intervention 2: Green Buffer

Plant a 10m urban forest canopy:

Permeable rain bioswales absorbing 90% of road runoff and cutting traffic noise by 8dB.

Intervention 3: Mobility Hub

Build a perimeter Park-and-Ride:

500 shared cargo e-bikes and frequent airport shuttle vans connecting to local tram terminus.

90-Second Redesign Pitch Framework

Structure your pitch with your partner using this 3-step formula:

1. Current Problem: "Currently, this 8-lane corridor creates severe air pollution and isolates airport workers..."
2. Redesign Solution: "By reallocating 4 lanes to electric BRT and active cycling, we cut emissions by 60%..."
3. Handling Objections: "Although motorists may complain about fewer lanes, commuter travel times actually drop..."

Part 6: High-Stakes Public Debate — The Car-Free City Center

Motion: "This city should permanently ban private fossil-fueled vehicles from the central district within 18 months, reallocating all street parking to parks and bike paths."

Role A: Suburban Commuters & Drivers

Strongly Opposes Blanket Ban:

  • Suburban families cannot afford city center rents and rely on cars to commute.
  • Suburban transit takes twice as long and stops early at night.
  • Delivery drivers and tradespeople face massive delays and parking fines.

Role B: Local Retailers & Restaurants

Demands Flexible Compromise:

  • Cleaner streets boost cafe terraces, but retailers fear losing suburban shoppers.
  • Demands free 30-minute delivery bays and large perimeter park-and-ride garages.
  • Proposes weekend-only pedestrianization before any permanent weekday ban.

Role C: Clean Air & Youth Coalition

Demands Total Immediate Ban:

  • Car pollution causes respiratory illness in children; streets belong to humans.
  • 70% of inner-city space is currently wasted on parked metal boxes.
  • European cities proved that businesses thrive when streets become pedestrianized.

Negotiated Municipal Policy Resolution

Collaborate with the other stakeholders to agree on a compromise resolution (e.g. exempted vehicles, phase-in timeline, perimeter parking):

Part 6 (Cont.): Technical Mastery Quiz & Final Self-Assessment

Check your understanding of double comparatives, contrast connectors, and sustainable urban mobility concepts.

1. What is the primary purpose of a "Sponge City"?
[   ] A. Cooling skyscrapers with air conditioning
[   ] B. Absorbing, filtering, and reusing rainwater
[   ] C. Building underground parking lots
2. Choose the correct double comparative:
[   ] A. The more cycle paths we build, safer commuters feel.
[   ] B. The more cycle paths we build, the safer commuters feel.
[   ] C. More cycle paths we build, the more safe commuters feel.
3. What does "Active Mobility" prioritize?
[   ] A. High-speed electric taxis
[   ] B. Walking, wheeling, and cycling
[   ] C. Autonomous flying drones
4. Select the formal contrast connector:
"____ high initial costs, the tramway cuts emissions."
[   ] A. Whereas   [   ] B. Despite   [   ] C. Unless
5. What is the Urban Heat Island effect?
[   ] A. Tropical island weather phenomena
[   ] B. Concrete absorbing heat, making cities hotter
[   ] C. Heat produced exclusively by airplane engines
6. What defines a "15-Minute City"?
[   ] A. Speed limit strictly 15 km/h across the city
[   ] B. Daily necessities reachable in 15 min on foot/bike
[   ] C. Free transit rides limited to 15 minutes
7. What is a "Superblock" in urban design?
[   ] A. Multi-story concrete parking facility
[   ] B. Street grid restricting through-traffic to perimeter
[   ] C. Giant shopping mall with no windows
8. Which mode sits at the TOP of the Mobility Hierarchy?
[   ] A. Walking, wheeling, and cycling
[   ] B. Shared electric kick-scooters
[   ] C. Single-occupancy electric luxury cars
9. What is the environmental benefit of High-Speed Rail over domestic air?
[   ] A. Cuts per-passenger corridor emissions by 85–95%
[   ] B. Guarantees 0-minute travel times between hubs
[   ] C. Eliminates all ticket fares for commuters
10. Complete: "The denser the transit network, ____"
[   ] A. fewer cars enter the city center.
[   ] B. the fewer cars enter the city center.
[   ] C. the less cars enter the city center.
